(Photo by Gavriil Grigorov / POOL / AFP) / image distributed by the Russian state owned agency Sputnik) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday that preliminary information indicates Russia used a North Korean ballistic missile in the strike on the village of Radushne that killed an entire family of 10. Zelensky provided the details in a statement on Telegram, just hours after the Russian missile strike on Radushne , in the Kryvyi Rih district of the Dnipropetrovsk region, killed two parents, along with their seven children and an 18-month old grandson. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “Of course, there will still be expert examinations, everything will be verified, but as of now, it is North Korean ballistics,” Zelensky said, adding that this is the first such use “in a long while.” According to two sources cited by Reuters, the strike marked the first suspected use of such a weapon in nearly a year. Advertisement The strike drew international reactions The strike drew condemnation worldwide, especially from allied countries. European countries also reacted to a separate incident, in which a Russian missile crossed into Polish territory , exploding in a field near Lublin during the same overnight barrage. While no casualties or damage were reported in Poland, Russia’s massive missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight Thursday, July 30, killed at least eight people and injured more than 35, including three children. A similar drone incident occurred over Romania’s territorial waters near the Sulina-Chilia area over the weekend on July 24-26, in which Romania scrambled a F-16 fighter jet to intercept a Russian-made Shahed drone. The interception marked the third such incident over the course of three consecutive days, prompting Romania’s foreign ministry ordered a Russian embassy employee to be expelled in what it called a “firm response” to drones repeatedly breaching the NATO member’s airspace along the Ukrainian border. Other Topics of Interest Crimea Bridge Closed as Explosions Rock Occupied Peninsula Russia temporarily closed the Kerch Bridge as explosions were reported across occupied Crimea and air defenses opened fire over Sevastopol. “Most importantly, though, is not just sympathy and not just condemnation, but missiles for air defense,” Zelensky said, renewing his appeal for much needed air defense systems. Advertisement North Korea’s deepening role in Russia’s war North Korea has become one of Russia’s most critical wartime partners, supplying troops, weapons and manpower in exchange for financial and technological support . Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) estimated that North Korea supplies between 25% and 40% of Russia’s artillery shells , while the two countries are also nearing completion of their first-ever road bridge over the Tumen River to ease supply flows. The first reported use of North Korean ballistic missiles by Russia dates back to Dec. 29, 2023, when one missile landed in a field in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region. Russia deployed the missiles again just days later, on Jan. 2, 2024, during a massive strike on Kharkiv that left two people dead and injured 62 others. “The alliance between the Moscow scumbags and the deranged regime in North Korea exists for the sake of missiles,” Zelensky said, accusing Pyongyang of “killing our Ukrainian children.” Moscow signed a defense pact with Pyongyang on June 19, 2024, with both countries officially recognizing North Korean troop deployments in April 2025. Zelensky warned Wednesday, July 29 that Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 additional North Korean troops and more ballistic missile launchers. Advertisement Patriot interceptors remain central Ukraine has repeatedly identified Patriot interceptors as one of its most urgent battlefield needs, citing critical shortages of the only weapon currently capable of intercepting Russia’s ballistic missiles. “Missiles for air defense, and above all missiles for the Patriots, but also for the NASAMS, for the IRIS-Ts, for the HAWKs, and our other systems,” remains a key priority, Zelensky said, adding that he counts “on all our partners, and above all our American partners,” for delivery. On Tuesday, Zelensky held what he called a “ productive meeting ” with US President Donald Trump in the Oval office at the White House, in which the two discussed advancing Patriot interceptor production, as well as the revival of stalled diplomacy with Russia. Trump first signaled he would grant Ukraine a license to produce the missiles during the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 7-8, however, it was floated only as an idea at the time. As of Tuesday, Zelensky confirmed that the plan had moved to concrete steps, with the US allowing Ukraine to produce the missiles domestically. Also onTuesday, Zelensky met with Lockheed Martin representatives to discuss expanding joint weapons production and technology sharing . Less than a week earlier, on July 23, Zelensky announced a possible joint cooperation with Raytheon as well, without providing a specific timeline for launching production. Advertisement On July 20, Lockheed Martin unveiled cheaper Patriot interceptors , PAC-3 ACE, designed to deter air and missile threats at less than half the cost of the PAC-3 MSE as global demand surges. https://www.dw.com/en/renee-good-s-famil.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Naq4 The deployment of federal border forces in Minneapolis in January led to protests, which were only amplified after the fatal shootings of Renee Good and another US citizen [FILE: January 11, 2026] Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS Advertisement Relatives of Renee Good, the 37-year-old woman shot dead in her car in Minneapolis by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent on January 7 this year, are suing the US government in a civil lawsuit connected to her death that was filed on Thursday. Good and her wife had been taking part in daily protests in the city against the deployment of armed and often masked federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest and identify undocumented migrants for deportation. The lawsuit alleges "federal conspiracy with discriminatory design and authorized use of force against observers," saying that this resulted in "extreme and unconstitutional force" being exerted against "people exercising their rights under the [US] constitution's Bill of Rights." Good's killing, followed two weeks later by the death of nurse Alex Pretti , intensified the already-sizeable protests against the deployment of ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents in Minneapolis known as Operation Metro Surge . The deaths of Renee Good and later Alex Pretti led to widespread protests in Minneapolis, and a winding-down of Operation Metro Surge, which ceased entirely by mid-February Image: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images What do the lawsuits allege? The plaintiffs in the twin civil suits from the Romanucci Blandin Law firm, filed on October 1 , are Good's brother Brent Ganger — acting as trustee for her other next of kin including her three children — and her partner Becca Good. One names the United States of America as the sole defendant. The other names a series of responsible government and border control officials, including but not limited to the ICE officer who shot Good in her car, White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, and the US Secretary of Homeland Security at the time of the shooting, Kristi Noem. "Renee's death was not an accident," Romanucci Blandin Law wrote in a statement. "It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest." Minnesota killing spurs backlash over ICE enforcement To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video They allege that Operation Metro Surge "was built on exaggerated fraud accusations that the White House embraced as a pretext for thousands of masked, unidentified federal agents to rove neighborhoods and stop people based on how they looked." It said that government officials "told agents to force confrontations with observers like Renee and led agents to believe that they would face no consequences for using force." The crackdown in Minneapolis, which has a large Somali population, came as part of President Donald Trump 's tough stance on migration and border security, and amid his assertions that local authorities in some Democrat-run states do an inadequate job fighting crime and irregular migration. 'She was pure love' Becca Good, Renee's wife, made her public comments about the shooting at a press conference in Minneapolis on Thursday. "I'm here today because last January the whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed," she said. Becca said of her wife: "She was pure love. She was ⁠funny. She ​was smart. She was gorgeous." "Renee believed in something simple: that being good can change the world," she added. "She believed everyone deserves love ​and compassion, care and dignity, no matter who they were or where they came from." Becca Good made her first public remarks since her wife was shot dead Image: Ellen Schmidt/AP Photo/picture alliance Brett Ganger, Renee Good's brother, said, "The hole in my family and myself created by my sister’s passing is hauntingly apparent". "What happened to Renee was completely senseless and the fact ​that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Ganger said. "What happened to America? Something must change now," he stressed. https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/world-news.text: Poland scrambled fighter jets after a Russian military helicopter crossed nearly 1,000ft into its airspace. The Mi-8 made a brief incursion near the Polish town of Braniewo after entering the country’s airspace from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the Polish military said. The helicopter spent about 42 seconds in Polish airspace at 11.08am local time on Wednesday, reaching a maximum depth of around 300 metres (984ft), according to Poland’s Operational Command of the Armed Forces. "Fighter jets were scrambled, and ground-based forces and assets remained on alert. The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence," the operational command said in a statement on X. "Polish air defence crews are conducting round-the-clock surveillance, remaining in a state of constant readiness to ensure the security of Polish airspace." Loud bangs from Polish F-16 fighter jets were heard across the Świętokrzyskie and Podkarpackie regions in south-east Poland. Authorities said the noise was caused by jets carrying out routine tasks to secure Polish airspace. It came just days after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned there was a "real risk" that Russia could launch "hybrid drone and missile strikes" against his country and other countries on NATO's eastern flank while presenting them as accidents. Tusk issued the warning in the Polish parliament on Thursday, citing intelligence assessments. He said such attacks could be intended to test NATO's willingness to invoke Article 5, which requires member states to come to the aid of an ally under attack. Meanwhile, Russia launched a barrage of drone strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday morning, hitting railway infrastructure, warehouses and fuel stations and killing at least seven people, including two in Kyiv. "Russians launched many drones against the city [Kyiv]," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on social media. "As of now, two people have been reported killed." Officials in Kyiv said 41 people had been wounded. At least four people were killed, including a young child, in a strike on a residential building in Oleksandrivka, west of Kramatorsk in the eastern Donbas region. The attacks came just hours after Zelensky, who is in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, met with US President Donald Trump to discuss efforts to end the war.

Across the Baltics, including in NATO and European Union member ​Latvia, many voters are on edge after official warnings of potential Russian aggression and a growing number ‌of airspace incursions related to Moscow’s war in Ukraine. Russia says accusations that it is planning to attack NATO are baseless and Western officials say it is not capable of launching a direct assault, but security concerns have weighed heavily in the election campaign. “The priority, in my view, is, of course, security – security in Latvia. And then… as a student, I’d say support for students, the economy, and also support for pensioners,” said Megija ‌Nordena, 21, ​from Riga. Opinion polls put Kulbergs’ centrist United List ahead, with about 14% of ⁠votes, but followed closely by the overtly ⁠pro-Russian Sovereign Power. A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray military drones flew undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials have blamed Russia for causing them to divert from their flight paths. “We have to give Ukraine everything necessary ​right now (so) that they can have the upper hand and win”, Kulbergs told Reuters in an interview. Throughout his campaign, he has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one ⁠of the highest levels in NATO. But his pro-Kremlin rivals say Latvia should ⁠stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the ​country’s Russian-speaking minority. “Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts”, party leader Julia ​Stepanenko told Reuters. “The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it… Ukraine ‌must win, but through peace talks”. Polls opened at 8 a.m. (0500 GMT) and are due to close at 8 p.m., with the first results expected within hours and the final result likely to be clear after midnight. The 100 members of the Saeima, or parliament, are being elected for a four-year term. DIVIDED NATION Surveys show at least two other parties may make it into parliament – the populist, ⁠MAGA-style Latvia First grouping and the Progressives, a left-leaning party that attracts younger voters. Kulbergs’ ability to forge a working coalition will depend largely on how many votes they receive and how many other parties cross the 5% threshold to enter parliament. He might ⁠also need to cobble together a deal with ‌Latvia First leader, businessman Ainars Slesers, who appears to have shifted towards a more ⁠anti-Ukraine stance in recent months, courting votes on both sides. “His message is that (the party) condemns ​Russia’s invasion ‌and stands with Ukraine, but that supporting Ukraine comes at the expense of Latvia’s ​economy,” said Roberts ⁠Kits, researcher for the Latvian Strategy and Economic Research Institute, in a note. The ethnic Russian minority in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life which many see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south, and Russia and Belarus to the east.
